newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland wins US investment but must look East - IDA.
newsitem.headline: Ireland wins US investment but must look East - IDA.

text.p: Ireland is market leader for U.S. firms undertaking greenfield investment in Europe but must compete more aggresively in the EU to win projects going to Eastern Europe, the government's development board said on Tuesday.
Kieran McGowan, Chief Executive of IDA Ireland, said in an end-year statement that 13,180 jobs were created in IDA-backed companies in 1996, the best-ever year for Irish job creation.
"With three very strong years behind us, Ireland has also become, for the first time, the market leader of U.S. companies undertaking greenfield investment into Europe.
He cited IBM, Citibank and Eastman Kodak among U.S. companies which have set up in Ireland, helped by grants and a 10 percent corporation tax rate for manufacturing companies.

"Thirty percent of all such projects now come to Ireland, an indicator of the very strong competitive position of the economy and endorsing the merits of the focused and aggressive marketing approach of IDA Ireland," he said.

But McGowan said Ireland had to "compete more aggresively than ever for German and other intra-European manufacturing projects as they now tend to favour locations in Eastern European countries. These projects in the past tended to favour rural locations in Ireland," he said.

McGowan said the costs of each job had declined in 1996 despite high competition - the average cost per job sustained over seven years is now 11,920 Irish pounds, down in real terms from 12,200 the previous year and one third of the price 10 years ago.
Total expenditure on IDA grants in 1996 was 136 million pounds, he said. Most of this was provided by the exchequer but substantial contributions were refunded from EU social and structural funds.
Job losses totalled 5,800 in 1996, mainly in a small number of large companies.
"It is as important to consolidate and sustain what we have already as to secure new greenfield projects for Ireland," he said.

"Most vulnerable currently are the labour intensive industries which have been here a long time and are facing ever-increasing competition from low-wage locations and technology driven businesses," he said.

McGowan said most of the new jobs were created in the electronics and information sectors while it was increasingly hard to secure new investment in clothing, textile or other labour intensive industry.
